theme: The fruit of the lips; diligence; the way of the upright
readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 12:1-14:35. These chapters continue the collection of contrasting sayings. As you read, look for what the proverbs say about the tongue, hard work, and the way that seems right.
settingTheScene: These chapters continue the first Solomonic collection. The sayings are brief, and they move quickly from subject to subject. They are not meant to be read all at once but to be pondered. Look for repeated themes: speech, work, the fear of the LORD, and the difference between appearance and reality. Some of the most quoted proverbs appear here.
observation: “Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid” (12:1).
“There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing” (12:18).
“Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad” (12:25).
“The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied” (13:4).
“Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm” (13:20).
“Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him” (13:24).
“There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death” (14:12).
“Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people” (14:34).
interpretation:
The sayings of these chapters circle around a few basic truths. First, the willingness to be corrected is the mark of the wise. “Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge.” The person who hates correction is called “stupid,” a strong word. It is a challenge to anyone who is touchy about criticism. Growth requires being willing to be told when we are wrong.

Second, words matter. Rash words are like swords, but wise words heal. The tongue can wound or it can restore. “A good word makes him glad.” A kind word to an anxious person is a gift. The book returns again and again to speech, because speech reveals and shapes the heart.

Third, the company we keep forms us. “Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise.” We become like those we spend time with. The proverb is a reminder to choose friendships carefully, and to be the kind of friend others can learn from.

The most searching proverb in the section is 14:12: “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.” It appears twice in the book (16:25). The danger is not only that we choose obvious wrong. It is that we are often convinced we are right. Self-deception is a serious problem, and it is why we need God’s word and wise counsel. We cannot trust our own sense of rightness.

The collection also includes strong statements on work, honesty, and the poor. “Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.” How we treat the poor is a statement about how we regard God. And there are sayings about the fear of the LORD as a fountain of life and a place of confidence.

The section ends with a corporate lesson: “Righteousness exalts a nation.” Moral character is not a private matter. It shapes whole societies.
connection: Jesus said that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34), and that we will give an account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36). He warned that many call the narrow way hard and choose the broad one (Matthew 7:13-14). Proverbs 14:31 is echoed in Matthew 25:40: “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” James 3 expands on the power of the tongue.
application:
Think of a recent conversation. Did your words wound or heal? Ask forgiveness if needed.

Examine your friendships. Who are you becoming like?

Ask God where you might have a “way that seems right” that leads somewhere else.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you a love for correction.
Ask him to make your words bring healing.
Ask him to show you the way that seems right but is not.
